candidate_sources.title: Alternaria black molds & stem cankers (ID, Control & Prevention Tips)
candidate_sources.snippet: Cankers appear on stems, leaves, and fruit, have dark brown to black color, and can lead to the death of a plant. Black molds appear as light to dark brown lesions on the surface of ripe fruits, that are later covered in a black layer.

candidate_sources.title: Diseases of Corn: Stalk Rots - Purdue Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Purdue Extension publication covering corn stalk rots and stem-related diseases, including fungal pathogens causing cankers and rots that girdle stems before harvest.

candidate_sources.title: Collar Rot and Alternaria Stem Canker of Tomato | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Dark brown to black cankers with concentric zonation occur on stems near the soil line or aboveground. Cankers enlarge, girdle the stem before harvest, and kill the plants. Dark brown to black areas of dead tissue between leaf veins are caused by a toxin produced by the fungus.

candidate_sources.title: Anthracnose leaf blight on corn | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Water-soaked, oval lesions with tan centers and reddish-brown borders. Lesions begin on lower corn leaves and develop on upper leaves late in season. Dark, raised spots (fruiting bodies) and spines appear on dead tissue. Caused by fungus Colletotrichum graminicola. Disease favors high temperatures and prolonged wet weather.

candidate_sources.title: Anthracnose in Corn | CropWatch | Nebraska
candidate_sources.snippet: Anthracnose is caused by the fungus Colletotrichum graminicola. The disease appears as leaf blight early in the season and develops into stalk rot as the plant matures. Three distinct phases include leaf blight, top die-back, and stalk rot. Management includes resistant varieties and crop rotation.

candidate_sources.title: Anthracnose Leaf Blight of Corn | Crop Protection Network
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive encyclopedia entry covering symptoms, pathogen biology of Colletotrichum graminicola, disease development conditions, and integrated management strategies. Lesions characterized by oval shape with tan centers and dark reddish-brown borders on corn leaves.

candidate_sources.title: Anthracnose Stalk Rot - Cornell CALS
candidate_sources.snippet: Caused by Colletotrichum graminicola. Disease symptoms appear as shiny, black discoloration in blotches or streaks on the stalk surface, particularly on lower internodes. Overwinters in corn residue. Management includes hybrid selection, residue management, and crop rotation.

candidate_sources.title: Corn Ear Rots and Mycotoxins - Penn State Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive guide covering identification and management of corn ear rot diseases, including Colletotrichum-associated ear rot. Discusses pathogen survival on crop residues and management strategies including resistant varieties and cultural practices.

candidate_sources.title: Anthracnose Stalk Rot of Corn - Crop Protection Network Encyclopedia
candidate_sources.snippet: Pathogen: Colletotrichum graminicola. Three phases of disease: leaf blight, top dieback, and stalk rot. Stalk rot symptoms include shiny black discoloration on lower internodes. Environmental conditions and hybrid resistance influence disease development and severity.

candidate_sources.title: Anthracnose in Corn - University of Kentucky IPM Program
candidate_sources.snippet: Integrated Pest Management guide for anthracnose caused by Colletotrichum graminicola. Covers identification of leaf blight, stalk rot and top dieback phases. Emphasizes scouting, resistant variety selection, residue management, and timely harvest as primary management strategies.

candidate_sources.title: Anthracnose Diseases in Corn - Bayer Crop Science
candidate_sources.snippet: Fungal pathogen Colletotrichum graminicola causes anthracnose with three main symptom phases: leaf blight, top dieback, and stalk rot. Management recommendations include hybrid selection, residue management, crop rotation, and scouting protocols.

candidate_sources.title: Top dieback in corn: Is anthracnose the cause?
candidate_sources.snippet: Top dieback symptoms appear as early as one to three weeks after tasseling with yellowed, purple or brown flag leaves. Anthracnose has three distinct phases: leaf blight, top die-back, and stalk rot. In fields with heavy anthracnose stalk rot pressure, a portion of the plant above the ears dies prematurely while the lower plant remains green. Pathogen: Colletotrichum graminicola.

candidate_sources.title: Anthracnose Leaf Blight
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive factsheet on anthracnose leaf blight of corn. Covers symptoms including water-soaked lesions on leaves with tan centers and reddish-brown borders, management strategies including resistant hybrids, cultural practices, and fungicide options. Caused by the fungus Colletotrichum graminicola.

candidate_sources.title: Aspergillus Ear Rot (BP-83-W)
candidate_sources.snippet: Aspergillus ear rot is caused by the fungal pathogen Aspergillus flavus. The disease is characterized by a dusty olive-green mold on kernels, appearing as patches of green to yellow spores on or between kernels. Symptoms can become dark olive green to brown as the ear rot ages. The ear rot is most common at the ear tips and often affects only a few kernels or small areas. Management includes selecting resistant hybrids with tight husks, harvesting at 20-25 percent moisture, and drying grain to 16 percent moisture or less immediately.

candidate_sources.title: Aspergillus Ear Rot and Aflatoxin Production
candidate_sources.snippet: Aspergillus ear rot is caused by Aspergillus flavus and is favored by hot (>86F) dry conditions at pollination and during grain fill. Infection occurs via kernel wounds or insect damage but fungal spores can also infect kernels by growing down the silk channel. Aflatoxin production increases as kernel moisture decreases, with highest production at 20-18 percent kernel moisture. Management strategies include selecting hybrids with tighter husks and favorable drought/heat stress characteristics, crop rotation with non-host crops, harvesting at 20-25 percent moisture, and cooling/drying grain immediately.

candidate_sources.title: Aspergillus Ear Rot of Corn
candidate_sources.snippet: Aspergillus ear rot is a fungal disease most commonly caused by Aspergillus flavus, appearing as an olive-green mold on kernels that may begin at the tip of the ear or be associated with injury from insects, birds, or hail. The disease is commonly observed during hot, dry years on stressed plants. If greater than 10 percent of ears show signs of Aspergillus ear rot, the field should be scheduled for early harvest. Conditions favoring infection include temperatures above 86°F, below-average rainfall, and nutrient deficiencies.

candidate_sources.title: Aspergillus Ear Rot in Corn
candidate_sources.snippet: University of Kentucky IPM Program guide to Aspergillus ear rot in corn, covering symptom identification, pathogen biology (Aspergillus flavus), disease conditions favoring infection, and integrated pest management strategies.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial brown spot of bean | Cornell Vegetables
candidate_sources.snippet: Small brown spots on leaves that coalesce with leaf yellowing; affected leaves develop shot-hole appearance. Pods have water-soaked spots with tiny white crusty centers. Pathogen: Pseudomonas syringae pv. syringae. Found on corn and other non-host plants in bean production areas.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Canker of Stone Fruit in the Home Fruit Planting
candidate_sources.snippet: Most conspicuous symptoms are cankers that exude gum during late spring and summer. Leaf infections appear as water-soaked spots becoming brown and dry, surrounded by yellow halos. Pathogen: Pseudomonas syringae species complex. Bacteria overwinter in canker margins and buds.

candidate_sources.title: Pseudomonas syringae pv. syringae (bacterial canker or blast (stone and pome fruits)) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI Compendium datasheet on P. syringae pv. syringae covering identity, distribution, diagnosis, biology and control measures. Causes bacterial canker/blast on stone fruits and pome fruits, and bacterial brown spot on legumes and corn.

candidate_sources.title: Xanthomonas vasicola pv. vasculorum (bacterial leaf streak of corn) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: Bacterial leaf streak of corn, caused by Xanthomonas vasicola pv. vasculorum, has been present in South Africa for over 70 years, but is an emerging disease of corn in North and South America. Management strategies include crop rotation to non-host crops, fall tillage for residue management, weed control, and use of resistant hybrids once screening is available.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Leaf Streak | CropWatch | Nebraska
candidate_sources.snippet: Initial symptoms appear as translucent, water-soaked streaks between veins and progress to longer yellowish to necrotic streaks. Bacterial leaf streak lesions have visible, bright yellow halos when backlit. Caused by Xanthomonas vasicola pv. vasculorum. Symptoms can range between one-to-several inches long and begin as narrow leaf lesions with wavy edges between corn leaf veins.

candidate_sources.title: Current Understanding of the History, Global Spread, Ecology, Evolution, and Management of the Corn Bacterial Leaf Streak Pathogen, Xanthomonas vasicola pv. vasculorum | Phytopathology®
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive peer-reviewed review covering the history, global spread, ecology, evolution, and management of the corn bacterial leaf streak pathogen Xanthomonas vasicola pv. vasculorum. Published in the American Phytopathological Society's Phytopathology journal, providing evidence-based research on this emerging disease affecting corn production globally.

candidate_sources.title: Goss's bacterial wilt and leaf blight on corn | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Elongated tan lesions with irregular margins extending parallel to veins. Dark water-soaked spots ('freckles') develop in lesions. Shiny patches of dried bacterial ooze appear similar to dry varnish. Systemic wilt phase with xylem discoloration, slimy stalk rot, wilting and plant death. Caused by Clavibacter michiganensis subspecies nebraskensis. Yield losses exceed 30% for susceptible hybrids. Management includes resistant hybrids, crop rotation, tillage burying residue, and grassy weed control.
diseases_mentioned: Goss's bacterial wilt and leaf blight

candidate_sources.title: Overview of Goss's Bacterial Wilt and Blight
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive overview of Goss's bacterial wilt and blight disease of corn. Covers symptoms, pathogen identification, epidemiology, and integrated management strategies for this major corn disease caused by Clavibacter michiganensis subspecies nebraskensis.

candidate_sources.title: Goss's Bacterial Blight Beginning to Show Up in Corn | South Dakota State University Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: South Dakota State University Extension resource on Goss's bacterial blight in corn. Details symptoms, disease identification, and management recommendations for preventing economic losses in corn production from this bacterial disease.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Stalk Rot | CropWatch | Nebraska
candidate_sources.snippet: Discoloration of leaf sheath and stalk at nodes; water-soaked, tan to brown lesions that become soft and mushy; foul odor; stalk rots completely and tops collapse. Caused by Erwinia carotovora strains. Favored by high temperatures and humidity.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Stalk Rot | University of Illinois Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Bacterial stalk rot caused by Erwinia chrysanthemi pv. zeae enters plants through wounds from hail, wind, or insect feeding. First and second internodes above soil appear water-soaked, develop tan-brown discoloration, and become soft. Management includes fall cultivation and avoiding excessive irrigation.

candidate_sources.title: Corn (Zea mays)-Bacterial Stalk Rot | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Stalk rot characterized by internal decay and soft, mushy tissue. Symptoms include sudden plant collapse with vascular strands remaining intact. Pathogen survives in plant residue. Transmission via bacterial infections through plant wounds.

candidate_sources.title: Management Suggestions for Barley Yellow Dwarf Virus Control
candidate_sources.snippet: Management suggestions include resistant varieties, weed management and timely planting can result in limited problems from this disease. Select small grain cultivars with documented resistance or tolerance for BYDV. Late fall planting of winter wheat and early planting of spring wheat can reduce infections since the aphids are less active.

candidate_sources.title: Barley Yellow Dwarf of Wheat, Oats, and Barley
candidate_sources.snippet: Symptoms on plants are most notable on the flag leaf and can be yellow, red, and/or purple, and infected plants may be stunted with decreased internode lengths. Reddish-purple or yellowish discoloration of the flag leaf is the most characteristic symptom of BYDV. The disease is caused by at least eight viral species that belongs to the Luteoviridae virus family, and it is transmitted by aphids.

candidate_sources.title: Reaction of Sweet Corn to Inoculation with Barley Yellow Dwarf Virus RMV-IL
candidate_sources.snippet: The reaction of five sweet corn hybrids to barley yellow dwarf virus (BYDV-RMV-IL) was determined. Symptoms were observed in three of the five hybrids in early plantings. Late plantings showed no symptoms observed in some hybrids, indicating timing affects symptom expression in corn.

candidate_sources.title: Physoderma Brown Spot
candidate_sources.snippet: University of Delaware Cooperative Extension factsheet providing detailed information on Physoderma Brown Spot disease of corn, including symptoms (small yellowish to brown lesions on leaves), pathogen identification, and management strategies

candidate_sources.title: Physoderma Brown Spot | CropWatch | Nebraska
candidate_sources.snippet: University of Nebraska Extension CropWatch publication on Physoderma Brown Spot affecting corn. Details disease symptoms, pathogen (Physoderma maydis), disease development in wet conditions, and survival in crop residue

candidate_sources.title: Physoderma brown spot of corn - PLANT DISEASE
candidate_sources.snippet: University of Illinois Extension plant disease factsheet on Physoderma brown spot. Describes small round to oval lesions (approximately 1/4 inch diameter) that appear as yellowish to brown spots on corn leaves, caused by the fungal pathogen Physoderma maydis

candidate_sources.title: Northern corn leaf spot | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Northern corn leaf spot is caused by Bipolaris carbonum (Cochliobolus carbonum). The disease affects corn foliage and ears, with tan to grayish lesions surrounded by darker borders. Favorable conditions include moderate temperature and high humidity with abundant sporulation in damp weather. Control includes resistant hybrids and crop rotation.

candidate_sources.title: Northern Corn Leaf Spot
candidate_sources.snippet: Northern corn leaf spot caused by Bipolaris carbonum shows symptoms as oval to circular tan spots with concentric zones (Race 1) or chocolate-colored oblong spots (Race 2), with both races attacking ears. Race 3 produces narrow linear lesions up to 15-20 cm long surrounded by darkly pigmented borders.

candidate_sources.title: Northern Corn Leaf Spot - Cornell CALS
candidate_sources.snippet: Northern corn leaf spot (Bipolaris carbonum) causes grayish tan lesions on lower leaf blades that are narrow and up to 1 inch long, surrounded by a darker border. The most effective controls are resistant hybrids combined with crop rotation and proper tillage management.

candidate_sources.title: Charcoal Rot / Corn / Agriculture: Pest Management Guidelines / UC Statewide IPM Program (UC IPM)
candidate_sources.snippet: Charcoal rot is caused by the soilborne fungus Macrophomina phaseolina. In North America, it is most prevalent in the Southern U.S. and Mexico, but can develop in the U.S. Corn Belt under favorable conditions. In cooler, moisture abundant regions, charcoal rot is less prolific and often not present in climates with temperatures below 85°F.

candidate_sources.title: Charcoal Rot - Purdue Agriculture
candidate_sources.snippet: Management of charcoal rot is dependent on crop rotation with less susceptible hosts. Production practices that promote good plant health including balanced fertilization, appropriate plant populations, and good water management can reduce stresses that predispose corn to stalk rot. There are no registered fungicides to control charcoal rot.

candidate_sources.title: Charcoal Rot in Corn | Pioneer® Seeds
candidate_sources.snippet: Charcoal rot causes shredded, gray stalk tissue with a silvery gray appearance due to the development of black microsclerotia. The pith and stalk rind tissue exhibit a charred appearance, with infection beginning as root rot spreading into lower stalk internodes. Disease development is favored by hot and dry conditions, typically when temperatures reach 80-85°F.

candidate_sources.title: Charcoal Rot / Corn / UC Statewide IPM Program
candidate_sources.snippet: University of California IPM pest management guidelines for charcoal rot in corn. Caused by Macrophomina phaseolina, a heat- and drought-favoring pathogen. Symptoms include early ripening, shredding and breaking at crown, with microsclerotia germinating at 30-35°C forming appresoria to penetrate host epidermis. Microsclerotia in soil can survive 15 years as primary inoculum source.

candidate_sources.title: Chocolate Spot of Corn in Minnesota
candidate_sources.snippet: Disease documented in dent corn plants in Minnesota in July 1981, caused by Pseudomonas syringae pv. coronafaciens, marking the first report of chocolate spot of corn outside of Wisconsin

candidate_sources.title: Watch for Bacterial Diseases in Corn | CropWatch | Nebraska
candidate_sources.snippet: Extension resource covering bacterial diseases affecting corn crops with identification and management information from Nebraska Extension and USDA Cooperative Extension
