candidate_sources.title: Holcus Spot on Corn | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive extension factsheet on Holcus spot (caused by Pseudomonas syringae pv. syringae) and other bacterial corn diseases from University of Minnesota Extension, a major Midwestern agricultural extension service

candidate_sources.title: Cladosporium Ear Rot | Troubleshooting Abnormal Corn Ears
candidate_sources.snippet: Cladosporium ear rot is characterized by scattered dark, green-black kernels throughout an ear that can appear slightly shriveled and may split open, revealing tufts of fungal growth. The dark green, fuzzy fungus grows on and between kernels, causing black streaks. The disease is caused by the saprophytic fungus Cladosporium herbarum and does not produce any known mycotoxins.

candidate_sources.title: Cladosporium Ear Rot of Corn
candidate_sources.snippet: Cladosporium ear rot may develop as dark (brown to green) fuzzy mold growing on and between kernels with black, irregular streaks. Wet weather near harvest favors the disease, and plants with damage from frost, hail, or insects are more susceptible to infection. Cultural controls that prevent kernel damage and timely insect management can help reduce infection rates.

candidate_sources.title: Corn ear rots and mycotoxins | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Cladosporium ear rot is caused by Cladosporium herbarum and is more common in hot, dry years in the northern Corn Belt. It can grow at temperatures higher than 90°F and grain moisture as low as 16 percent. Management strategies include crop rotation, heavy tillage, planting insect-resistant hybrids, proper grain storage at 13-14% moisture content, and discarding susceptible varieties.

candidate_sources.title: Cladosporium herbarum | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI Compendium datasheet on Cladosporium herbarum covering Identity, Distribution, Hosts/Species Affected including maize/corn, and Further Information. Provides comprehensive information on the fungal pathogen and its relationships with various host crops including corn.

candidate_sources.title: Common Rust of Corn | Ohioline
candidate_sources.snippet: Common rust of corn is caused by the fungus Puccinia sorghi. Symptoms appear as reddish-brown, powdery pustules on corn leaves that are easily recognized by their dark appearance. Pustules develop within 7 days after infection under favorable conditions (cool temperatures 60-76°F, high humidity >95%, and 6+ hours leaf wetness). Management relies on planting resistant corn hybrids.

candidate_sources.title: Common rust on corn | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Common rust is caused by Puccinia sorghi and begins as yellow flecks that develop into oval to elongate reddish-brown pustules on corn leaves. The pustules are less than 1/4 inch long and darken over time. Disease development is favored by cool, wet conditions. Resistant varieties and fungicide applications at disease threshold (80% of leaves with pustules) are primary management strategies.

candidate_sources.title: Corn Rusts: Common and Southern Rust | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: This publication covers both common rust (Puccinia sorghi) and southern rust (Puccinia polysora) of corn. Common rust pustules are smaller, more uniform in size, and arranged in neat rows on leaves, favoring cooler temperatures. Southern rust pustules are larger and more scattered. Management includes cultivar selection for resistance and timely fungicide applications.

candidate_sources.title: Common smut on corn | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Common smut of corn is caused by the fungus Ustilago maydis. Galls can appear anytime throughout the growing season on any above ground plant part, commonly developing on ears, leaves, stalk, or tassels and are initially covered with white to silvery tissue. Later, dark masses of spores develop inside the galls. The most obvious symptoms are tumor-like galls that vary in size from less than 1 cm to more than 30 cm in diameter.

candidate_sources.title: Common smut of corn
candidate_sources.snippet: Common smut, caused by the fungus Ustilago maydis, is a disease of corn that occurs worldwide. Young tissue of corn plants is predisposed to infection. Smut galls develop where the fungus penetrates the plant tissue. The fungus remains viable in crop residue for several years and can be spread by wind, insects, or contaminated equipment.

candidate_sources.title: Common Smut on Corn | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Common smut is caused by the fungus Ustilago maydis. The disease can be managed through cultural practices including removal of affected plant parts before they release spores, selection of resistant varieties when available, and avoiding plant injury from hail or mechanical damage. Excessive nitrogen fertilization may increase disease severity.

candidate_sources.title: Corn Smut | Yard and Garden
candidate_sources.snippet: Corn smut disease characterized by gall formations on any above-ground plant part. Young, actively growing tissue especially susceptible. Disease management includes resistant varieties, removal of galls, and crop rotation practices.

candidate_sources.title: Common Corn Smut – Wisconsin Horticulture
candidate_sources.snippet: Fungal disease affecting corn with galls appearing on ears, tassels, and other plant tissues. Pathogen persists in soil and crop residue. Management strategies include cultural practices and selection of resistant corn varieties.

candidate_sources.title: Spiroplasma kunkelii (corn stunt spiroplasma) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI's comprehensive datasheet on Spiroplasma kunkelii, the causal agent of corn stunt disease. Details pathogen biology, transmission by corn leafhopper vector (Dalbulus maidis), distribution, and disease management strategies.

candidate_sources.title: Corn Leafhopper Leads to Corn Stunt Disease Across Oklahoma – August 12, 2024 | Oklahoma State University
candidate_sources.snippet: Extension pest alert documenting corn stunt disease symptoms including stunting, short internodes, leaf streaking, multiple small ears, reddening of leaves, and poor kernel fill. Details transmission by corn leafhopper and current outbreak across Oklahoma counties.

candidate_sources.title: Association of the Pathogen Spiroplasma kunkelii with Corn Stunt Symptoms in Oklahoma, Kansas, Missouri, Arkansas, Nebraska, South Dakota, New York, Wisconsin, Minnesota, Indiana, and Alabama During the 2024 Growing Season | Plant Health Progress
candidate_sources.snippet: APS peer-reviewed publication confirming widespread geographic distribution of Spiroplasma kunkelii in 11 states across 2024 growing season, with detailed symptomatology including leaf chlorosis, reddening, axillary buds, plant stunting, and 'loose tooth ears' from kernel deformation.

candidate_sources.title: Crazy Top Disease Developing in Corn - SDSU Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Crazy top is caused by Sclerophthora macrospora, an oomycete downy mildew. Symptoms include excessive tillering, rolling and twisting of upper leaves, and proliferation of the tassel into a mass of leafy structures. Infection occurs when soils are saturated for 24-48 hours shortly after planting, allowing overwintering oospores to germinate and produce zoospores that swim in water to infect young corn plants. Management includes improved drainage and avoiding planting in low, wet spots.

candidate_sources.title: Signs of Crazy Top in Corn - Integrated Crop Management
candidate_sources.snippet: Crazy top causes excessive tillering and shortened internodes in corn. Leaves may be narrow, strap-like, or show chlorotic striping in severely infected plants. The characteristic symptom is a 'leafy' tassel instead of a normal tassel. The disease develops when soil is flooded shortly after planting or before the four to five leaf stage. It is caused by an oomycete pathogen (Sclerophthora macrospora) that survives in soil as oospores.

candidate_sources.title: Crazy Top of Corn - Plant Pathology
candidate_sources.snippet: Crazy top is an oomycete disease caused by Sclerophthora macrospora. Infected plants show distortion through excessive tillering and proliferation of the tassel with leafy structures. Leaves are narrow and leathery with possible long yellow stripes. Disease occurs with soil saturation shortly after planting. The pathogen survives as oospores in soil. Management relies on improved drainage and avoiding low, wet field areas. Pulling infected plants reduces inoculum buildup for subsequent seasons.

candidate_sources.title: Frequently Asked Questions about Crown Rot in Corn
candidate_sources.snippet: Crown rot is a complex disease where infection takes place in seedlings early in the season, but symptoms often do not become apparent until mid-season or nearing maturity. Symptoms include stunted growth, wilting, and discoloration of the lower leaves resulting from infection of vascular tissue in the crown. The interior pith of the crown will be discolored with tan-to-brown coloration observed with Fusarium infection.

candidate_sources.title: Fusarium Root and Crown Rot Developing in Corn
candidate_sources.snippet: Root and crown rots developing in corn after the seedling stage are usually caused by Fusarium spp. Crown rot of corn is commonly attributed to pathogens in the Fusarium genus, although the exact species or complex of species that cause it has yet to be determined. Management strategies include selection of corn products with tolerance or resistance, proper fertilizer recommendations, and addressing soil drainage issues.

candidate_sources.title: Post Emergent Damping Off of Corn Prevalent in Some Fields
candidate_sources.snippet: Post-emergent damping off of corn causes rotting of stems at or near the soil line with brown and soft lesions. Infected seedlings show yellowing and wilting of leaves. Multiple soil-borne pathogens cause damping off including Fusarium spp., Pythium spp., and Rhizoctonia spp., with symptoms most severe in cool, wet soil conditions below 55°F.

candidate_sources.title: Seed Rot and Damping-Off / Corn / UC Statewide IPM Program
candidate_sources.snippet: Seed rot and damping-off cause death of seedlings before or shortly after emergence. Pythium species cause dark, slimy lesions with root or mesocotyl shrivel and cortex rot. Damping-off favored by wet, cold soils and excessive water saturation. Management includes seed treatments, improved drainage, reduced seeding depth, and variety selection for disease resistance.

candidate_sources.title: Review of Pythium Species Causing Damping-Off in Corn
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive review of 14+ Pythium species identified as causing seed rot prior to germination or infecting young corn seedlings. Details pathogen characteristics, epidemiology, and disease management strategies for Pythium-associated damping-off in corn production systems.

candidate_sources.title: Diplodia Stalk Rot - University of Illinois Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Caused by Stenocarpella (Diplodia) maydis. Symptoms include white mycelium in lower stalks, tiny black specks (pycnidia) embedded in rind of lower stalk with lower, inner stalk having shredded tissue. Overwinters on corn debris and occurs after pollination.

candidate_sources.title: Diplodia Leaf Streak of Corn: A Diagnostic Guide - Plant Health Progress (APS)
candidate_sources.snippet: Diagnostic guide for Diplodia leaf streak caused by Stenocarpella macrospora. Young DLS lesions appear as long narrow streaks that can expand across leaf veins with elliptical shape, distinguishing from gray leaf spot lesions which remain narrow and restricted by leaf veins.

candidate_sources.title: Stenocarpella maydis (ear rot of maize) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI Compendium datasheet on Stenocarpella maydis covers Identity, Overview, Distribution, Dispersal, Hosts/Species Affected, Diagnosis, Biology & Ecology, Seedborne Aspects, Impacts, Prevention/Control, and Further Information. The fungus causes ear rot recognized as white mold beginning at the base of the ear that eventually becomes grayish-brown and rots the entire ear.

candidate_sources.title: Extension & Outreach :: Crop Sciences Department :: College of ACES, University of Illinois - Diplodia Ear Rot
candidate_sources.snippet: University of Illinois Extension factsheet providing comprehensive information on Diplodia ear rot identification, symptoms, pathogen biology, conditions favoring disease, and management strategies for corn growers.

candidate_sources.title: Timing and Efficacy of Fungicide Applications for Diplodia Ear Rot Management in Corn | Plant Health Progress
candidate_sources.snippet: Peer-reviewed research on fungicide management of Diplodia ear rot caused by Stenocarpella maydis and S. macrospora, examining timing of applications and efficacy in reducing ear rot severity and improving corn yield.

candidate_sources.title: Diplodia Ear Rot | Agronomic Crops Network
candidate_sources.snippet: Ohio State University extension article on Diplodia ear rot symptoms including white mold at ear base becoming grayish-brown, with details on the fungal structures (pycnidia) visible on husks and kernels.

candidate_sources.title: Diplodia Stalk & Ear Rot | Kansas State University Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Kansas State University extension publication by graduate student Bethany Grabow covering both stalk and ear rot symptoms, pathogen identification, and management recommendations for corn.

candidate_sources.title: MAIZE :: MAJOR DISEASES :: DOWNY MILDEW
candidate_sources.snippet: Downy mildew of maize causes chlorotic streaks on leaves, stunted and bushy plant appearance, shortening of internodes, and white downy growth on the lower surface of leaves. Severe chlorosis in upper leaves, stunting, deformation, and lodging occur. Infections may lead to death in susceptible varieties.

candidate_sources.title: Recovery Plan for Philippine Downy Mildew and Brown Stripe Downy Mildew of Corn
candidate_sources.snippet: Philippine Downy Mildew (PDM) caused by Peronosclerospora maydis is a major constraint to corn production. Annual yield losses in the Philippines were often 40 to 60% on farms before resistant varieties were widely available. On sweet corn, losses of 100% have been reported.

candidate_sources.title: Peronosporaceae species causing downy mildew diseases of Poaceae, including nomenclature revisions and diagnostic resources
candidate_sources.snippet: Graminicolous downy mildews (GDMs) caused by multiple Peronosporaceae genera affect maize, millets, sorghum, and sugarcane. Peronosclerospora and Sclerophthora species cause downy mildew on corn and rice. These pathogens cause severe losses in tropical climates, particularly in developing countries.

candidate_sources.title: Plant Pest Factsheet Emerging Pests of maize
candidate_sources.snippet: Dry rot and leaf spot of maize is documented as an emerging pest concern in maize. Stalk rot symptoms include 1-10 cm long brown lesions on the stalk and leaves, and wilting, discoloration and drying. The disease can turn the entire ear greyish-brown and shrunken, with white mould found between the grains. Management through crop rotations and deep ploughing of crop debris.

candidate_sources.title: Gibberella zeae (headblight of maize) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI's authoritative datasheet on Gibberella zeae, the primary causal agent of ear rot and stalk rot in maize. Covers pathogen biology, host range, symptoms on ears and stalks including pinkish discoloration and tissue necrosis, and management approaches including cultural and chemical control.

candidate_sources.title: Corn Ear Rots: Managing Mold and Mycotoxins | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: NC State Extension publication providing detailed symptom descriptions of ear rot diseases, associated pathogenic organisms, management practices, and mycotoxin concerns in corn.

candidate_sources.title: Occurrence and Management of the Emerging Pathogen Epicoccum sorghinum
candidate_sources.snippet: Epicoccum sorghinum is an emerging necrotrophic fungal pathogen that was originally characterized as a sorghum pathogen. E. sorghinum shows a broad host spectrum and can infect corn (maize), soybean, rice, and wheat. The pathogen causes leaf spot symptoms on a wide range of plants, leading to devastating losses in crop production and quality. E. sorghinum has been reported to biosynthesize the carcinogenic mycotoxin tenuazonic acid (TEA). There is currently no commercial antifungal agent to manage E. sorghinum.

candidate_sources.title: Epicoccum nigrum (red blotch of grains) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: Epicoccum nigrum is a saprophytic fungus that forms pustules composed of sporodochia and conidia on dead and dying plants. It invades various parts of dead plants including seeds of corn, barley, oats, and wheat. Epicoccum nigrum is known to cause red blotch of grains and has been identified as a causal agent of corn fungal leaf diseases.

candidate_sources.title: First Report of Epicoccum sorghinum Causing Leaf Sheath and Leaf Spot on Maize in China
candidate_sources.snippet: Epicoccum sorghinum produces small ellipse- and spindle-shaped spots on maize leaves, with the lesion center being grayish yellow to dark gray and surrounded by a chlorotic area. In severe cases, physiologically mature plants exhibit red-brown lesions in stem and leaves, and dried-up stems. Fungicide sensitivities vary, and management options include synthetic fungicides, plant extracts, and microbial biocontrol agents.

candidate_sources.title: Eyespot on corn | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Eyespot is caused by the fungus Kabatiella zeae. First visible symptoms are small, circular spots (1/16 inch to 1/8 inch diameter) that are water-soaked with yellow halos on leaves, which develop into an 'eyespot'—a tan spot surrounded by a brown to purple ring and narrow yellow halo. High disease levels occur in seed production fields, under no-till conditions, and when corn is planted sequentially. Management includes crop rotation with nonhost crops, selecting resistant hybrids, and considering foliar fungicide applications based on economics.

candidate_sources.title: Kabatiella zeae (eyespot) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: Kabatiella zeae is the causative pathogen of corn eyespot disease, an important leaf disease that damages corn (Zea mays L.) worldwide. K. zeae belongs to order Tuberculariales, class Hyphomycetes, genus Kabatiella. The CABI datasheet covers Identity, Overview, Distribution, Dispersal, Hosts/Species Affected, Diagnosis, Biology & Ecology, Seedborne Aspects, Impacts, and Prevention/Control. Diagnosis involves collecting leaf samples with typical eyespot symptoms and isolating the pathogen using PDA medium.

candidate_sources.title: Eyespot of Corn | Crop Protection Network
candidate_sources.snippet: Eyespot is a fungal disease caused by Kabatiella zeae that affects corn. The disease is most common in northern areas of the Midwest and is residue-borne. Cool temperatures (60s°F to low 70s°F), humidity, wet conditions, continuous corn, and conservation tillage favor disease development. Management strategies include crop rotation, hybrid selection for resistance, and careful evaluation of fungicide applications considering yield potential and crop value.

candidate_sources.title: Major Fusarium Diseases on Corn, Wheat, and Soybeans in the Corn Belt
candidate_sources.snippet: F. graminearum causes Gibberella stalk rot, ear rot, and kernel rot. F. moniliforme causes ear, stalk and foliage diseases. Symptoms include brown discoloration of pith, sheath rot with black spots and wet blotches. Root and crown rot causes wilting. Management includes crop rotation, resistance hybrids, and sanitation.

candidate_sources.title: Fusarium Ear Rot - UC Statewide IPM Program
candidate_sources.snippet: White to pink or purple cottony mold appears on ear; affected kernels are scattered and discolored (tan-brown) or have white streaks. Fusarium verticillioides and related species infect via silks or insect injury. Disease severity increases in warm regions with insect, hail, or other ear damage. Hybrids with tight husks and insect protection traits provide resistance.

candidate_sources.title: Fusarium Stalk Rot of Corn - Crop Protection Network
candidate_sources.snippet: Internal pith tissue shreds and discoloration becomes pinkish or salmon colored as rot progresses. Lower stem becomes soft and collapses. Disease begins after pollination and worsens as plant matures. Warm temperatures (80-100°F) and wet midseason following dry early season favor development. Management includes balanced fertility, crop rotation, hybrid resistance selection.

candidate_sources.title: Major Fusarium Diseases on Corn, Wheat, and Soybeans in the U.S.
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive extension guide covering Fusarium diseases including ear rot, stalk rot, and kernel rot in corn. Details on pathogen biology, symptoms, environmental conditions favoring disease, and management strategies including resistant varieties and crop rotation.

candidate_sources.title: Gibberella Ear Rot and Mycotoxins in Corn: Sampling, Testing, and Storage
candidate_sources.snippet: Ohio State University factsheet on Gibberella ear rot (caused by Fusarium graminearum/Gibberella zeae). Covers symptoms of pinkish-white mold at ear tip and silk channel infection, mycotoxin production (deoxynivalenol/DON/vomitoxin), environmental conditions during silking, and management recommendations.

candidate_sources.title: Why All The Fuss With The Plant Pathogen Fusarium Graminearum?
candidate_sources.snippet: Purdue University Extension newsletter article examining Fusarium graminearum as a major plant pathogen affecting corn and other cereals. Discusses pathogen characteristics, disease development, economic impact, and integrated management approaches.

candidate_sources.title: Fusarium crown and root rot | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Fusarium symptoms tend to be tan-to-reddish brown leathery lesions that cause the root or mesocotyl to shrivel. If seedlings continue to contend with wet conditions, Fusarium infections can persist and move into the crown and stalk tissues.

candidate_sources.title: An Overview of Ear Rots
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive overview of multiple ear rot diseases affecting corn, covering identification, symptoms, pathogens (Fusarium, Gibberella, Diplodia, Aspergillus, Penicillium, Stenocarpella), and management strategies for mixed ear rot infections.

candidate_sources.title: L741 Stalk Rots of Corn and Sorghum - Kansas State University
candidate_sources.snippet: Kansas State University extension publication (L741) detailing stalk rot diseases of corn, including symptom identification, fungal and bacterial pathogens, and integrated management recommendations for field crops.

candidate_sources.title: Common Stalk Rot Diseases of Corn - University of Nebraska-Lincoln Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Extension publication (EC1898) from University of Nebraska-Lincoln covering common stalk rot diseases of corn, including symptom descriptions, disease cycles, and management practices. Addresses multiple pathogenic fungi affecting corn stalks.

candidate_sources.title: Genetic Disorders of Corn: Genetic Flecking and Lesion Mimic
candidate_sources.snippet: Genetic disorders of corn, often referred to as genetic flecking and lesion mimic, are non-infectious (abiotic) conditions. Symptoms may appear as small water-soaked circular lesions that turn yellow to brown in color, long narrow lesions that are tan and dried in appearance, lesions with a mosaic pattern and dark concentric rings, or white or yellow streaks which result when cells in affected plants produce less chlorophyll.

candidate_sources.title: What causes striped corn leaves?
candidate_sources.snippet: Some corn hybrids are prone to genetic striping, which usually shows up on scattered plants in a field and tends to disappear over time. Leaf flecking is a mild lesion phenotype observed on the leaves of some maize lines. Genetic flecking and lesion mimic are non-infectious (abiotic) disorders that result in symptoms similar to many other foliar fungal or viral diseases of corn.

candidate_sources.title: Leaf Discolorations in Corn
candidate_sources.snippet: Leaf spots of corn in the United States can be caused by pathogens, herbicide injury, physiological, environmental, insects or genetic flecking. Genetic flecking is a non-infectious (abiotic) disorder. Disease lesion mimics are a class of mutants (Les/les genes) that can result in lesion development without the presence of a disease. Scientists have identified more than 50 lesion mimic mutations in corn.

candidate_sources.title: Disease Lesion Mimic Identified in Corn
candidate_sources.snippet: Disease lesion mimics are a class of mutants (Les/les genes) that can result in lesion development without the presence of a disease. Symptoms of DLM vary from tiny spots to lesions along the entire leaf, with lesions varying in color from chlorotic, to dark brown to translucent. Environmental stresses can be a trigger for these lesions. Since symptoms are caused by a genetic mutation and not a fungal pathogen, fungicides have no effect.

candidate_sources.title: Corn Diseases and Disorders
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive guide to corn diseases and disorders including genetic and nutritional causes of striping symptoms in corn leaves. Covers identification and management of various corn conditions.

candidate_sources.title: Diseases of Corn - Purdue Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Purdue Extension bulletin covering corn disease identification and management, including discussion of genetic and non-pathogenic causes of leaf striping and discoloration in corn.

candidate_sources.title: Gibberella Ear Rot and Mycotoxins in Corn: Sampling, Testing, and Storage
candidate_sources.snippet: Extension factsheet covering Gibberella ear rot caused by Gibberella zeae (Fusarium graminearum), characterized by pink to reddish mold at ear tip, infection via silk channel during cool wet weather post-silking, and associated mycotoxins including deoxynivalenol (DON/vomitoxin)

candidate_sources.title: Gibberella and Fusarium Ear Rots Developing in Corn
candidate_sources.snippet: South Dakota State University Extension article on development and identification of Gibberella and Fusarium ear rots in corn, including symptom recognition and management strategies

candidate_sources.title: Gibberella Ear Rot - UT Crops Pest Guides
candidate_sources.snippet: University of Tennessee Crops Pest Guide dedicated to Gibberella ear rot identification, biology, and integrated pest management approaches for corn production

candidate_sources.title: Goss's Bacterial Wilt and Leaf Blight of Corn
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive extension publication on Goss's disease caused by Clavibacter michiganensis subspecies nebraskensis. Details symptoms on leaves and stalks, disease epidemiology, and management strategies including selection of resistant hybrids, crop rotation with non-host crops (soybean, beans, small grains), tillage to bury residue, and weed control.

candidate_sources.title: Goss's Bacterial Wilt and Leaf Blight of Corn | Purdue Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Purdue Extension bulletin on Goss's wilt caused by the bacterium Clavibacter michiganensis subspecies nebraskensis. Covers identification of symptoms (lesions, freckles, vascular discoloration), disease conditions and spread, and management including hybrid selection, residue management, and cultural practices.

candidate_sources.title: Gray Leaf Spot - Purdue Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Gray leaf spot is caused by the fungal pathogen Cercospora zeae-maydis. The disease starts as small necrotic light-tan spots that expand into rectangular shapes, reaching up to 2 inches, limited within leaf veins. The diagnostic symptom of gray leaf spot is the sharp parallel edges of the lesion. Disease management includes using resistant corn hybrids, conventional tillage, crop rotation, and foliar fungicides if economically warranted.

candidate_sources.title: Gray leaf spot on corn | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Lesions appear as yellow or tan rectangular spots with darkened margins, and as lesions mature, they elongate and become more gray in color as spores are produced. Gray leaf spot (GLS) is caused by the ascomycete fungus, Cercospora zeae-maydis. In late spring, when conditions are warm (70-90°F) and humid (≥ 90%), the fungus will produce asexual spores (conidia) that are spread by wind to the lower leaves of growing corn plants.

candidate_sources.title: Gray Leaf Spot in Corn | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Gray leaf spot (GLS) is a foliar fungal disease that affects corn, caused by fungal pathogens including Cercospora zeae-maydis and Cercospora zeina. Distinct symptoms are rectangular, brown to gray necrotic lesions that run parallel to the leaf, spanning the spaces between secondary leaf veins. Disease development is favored by warm temperatures of 80°F and high humidity of 90% or higher for 12 hours or more.

candidate_sources.title: Corn Mold | Extension | West Virginia University
candidate_sources.snippet: Penicillium seedling blight is caused by the fungus Penicillium oxalicum, where a bluish-green mold develops on seed causing roots to deteriorate and seedling leaves turn yellow and may die, favored by wet and cool (55° F or lower) soils.

candidate_sources.title: Penicillium Ear Rot of Corn
candidate_sources.snippet: Green or blue-green powdery mold indicative of Penicillium ear rot usually begins at the tip of the ear. Management includes using high quality seed and good cultural practices such as planting seed in warm soil (above 55 °F), preparing seedbed properly, optimum water management.

candidate_sources.title: Head Smut / Corn / Agriculture: Pest Management Guidelines / UC Statewide IPM Program
candidate_sources.snippet: Head smut is caused by the fungus Sporisorium reilianum that systemically infects corn seedlings through the soil but does not show symptomology until later in reproductive stages when floral structures (tassels and ears) are converted to sori containing masses of powdery teliospores.

candidate_sources.title: Corn (Zea mays) - Head Smut | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Head smut produces thin strands covered in black spores mainly on tassels and ears. The cob is replaced by white sori which are structures that make and hold the spores of the fungus. Initial infections occur on roots of young seedlings, and the pathogen develops systemically.

candidate_sources.title: Identification and Management of Corn Head Smut | Crop Science US
candidate_sources.snippet: Head smut infects plants systemically while common smut only causes local infection. Management strategies include seed treatment with fungicides before planting, crop rotation, soil fertility management (avoiding nitrogen deficiency), and selecting resistant hybrids. The pathogen prefers dry soils and temperatures between 70-82°F.

candidate_sources.title: Seeing Spots on Corn? It's Likely Holcus Leaf Spot | NC State Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Holcus Leaf Spot is a bacterial disease of corn caused by Pseudomonas syringae pv. syringae. The disease is characterized by small, round to elliptical lesions with tan to white centers and red to brown margins. Lesions typically start on lower leaves and may be surrounded by yellow halos. Management notes that Holcus leaf spot is generally superficial and does not negatively impact corn yield potential.

candidate_sources.title: Holcus Spot | Illinois Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Holcus spot is a bacterial disease caused by Pseudomonas syringae pv. syringae. Symptoms include water-soaked dark green lesions near leaf tips that develop into tan spots with red-brown margins, 1/8 to 1/4 inch in diameter. The disease requires wounds for entry, typically from hail, wind, or thunderstorms, and thrives in warm, wet conditions. Management includes weedy host management and tillage, though there are no in-season control options.

candidate_sources.title: Khuskia oryzae (cob rot of maize) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: Khuskia oryzae causes cob and stalk rot of maize. Symptoms develop towards maturity mostly on the shanks, husks and ears but also on the stems and stalks, where blackish, shallow lesions can occur. Ears may snap off at harvest; the cob becomes shredded and rotten through disintegration of the parenchyma.

candidate_sources.title: Khuskia oryzae (cob rot of maize) - CABI ISC Database
candidate_sources.snippet: Khuskia oryzae is a fungal pathogen causing cob rot of maize. On maize, symptoms develop towards maturity mostly on the shanks, husks and ears but also on the stems and stalks, where blackish, shallow lesions develop. The fungus is of agricultural significance affecting yield through cob deterioration and ear breakage at harvest.

candidate_sources.title: Khuskia oryzae (cob rot of maize) - PlantWise Plus Knowledge Bank
candidate_sources.snippet: Khuskia oryzae causes cob and stalk rot of maize with symptoms on shanks, husks, ears, stems and stalks characterized by blackish shallow lesions. Infected ears are more likely to snap off at harvest; the maize cob shows clear signs of rotting with sparse mycelium and sporulation developing in the furrows between kernels.

candidate_sources.title: Northern Corn Leaf Blight - Purdue Extension BP-84-W
candidate_sources.snippet: Northern corn leaf blight (NCLB) is caused by the fungus Exserohilum turcicum. Typical symptoms are canoe-shaped lesions 1-6 inches long with gray-green borders that turn tan. Disease is most prevalent at 64-80°F with prolonged leaf wetness. Severe outbreaks can cause 30-50% yield loss if established before tassel.

candidate_sources.title: Northern Corn Leaf Blight - University of Minnesota Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Northern corn leaf blight (NCLB) is a fungal disease of corn caused by Exserohilum turcicum. Long, narrow tan lesions develop parallel to leaf margins with classic cigar-shaped appearance. Fungicide application recommended at tasseling (VT-R1) if disease present on 3rd leaf below ear leaf or higher on 50% of plants.

candidate_sources.title: Northern Corn Leaf Blight - Ohio State University
candidate_sources.snippet: Northern corn leaf blight (NCLB), caused by the fungus Exserohilum turcicum, is an increasingly important disease in the U.S. Corn Belt. Cultural practices including crop rotation and resistant varieties are primary control measures. Minimum one-year rotation from corn recommended for tilled fields.

candidate_sources.title: Northern Corn Leaf Blight | University of Delaware
candidate_sources.snippet: Northern corn leaf blight (NCLB) is caused by the fungus Exserohilum turcicum. Characteristic symptoms are one-to-six inch long cigar-shaped gray- to tan-colored lesions on leaves. Disease development favored by heavy dew, frequent rainfall, and high humidity. Infection occurs when free water is present on leaf surface for 6-18 hours at temperatures between 66-80°F.

candidate_sources.title: Maize Chlorotic Dwarf of Maize | Ohioline
candidate_sources.snippet: Maize chlorotic dwarf of maize is caused by Maize chlorotic dwarf virus (MCDV). Symptoms include plant stunting, shortening of upper internodes, leaf reddening or yellowing, leaf twisting and tearing, and vein banding. MCDV is mainly transmitted by the black-faced leafhopper Graminella nigrifrons. Control of Johnsongrass is the best way to avoid the disease.

candidate_sources.title: Maize Chlorotic Dwarf Virus | University of Illinois Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Maize chlorotic dwarf of maize is caused by Maize chlorotic dwarf virus (MCDV). Diverse symptoms include plant stunting, shortening of upper internodes, leaf reddening or yellowing, leaf twisting and tearing, and chlorosis or clearing of the smallest visible leaf veins (vein banding). MCDV has been reported from Texas up to Missouri and Ohio, covering 19 states of the United States and Mexico.

candidate_sources.title: Maize chlorotic dwarf virus | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: MCDV is mainly found in regions where an overlapping distribution of Johnsongrass, the overwintering virus host, and the maize leafhopper Graminella nigrifrons, its main vector, occurs. Seed treatment with systemic insecticide produces optimum efficacy against the leafhopper and other pests. MCDV caused severe economic losses in the Midwest and Southern United States during the 1960s to 1970s.

candidate_sources.title: Maize Dwarf Mosaic of Maize | Ohioline
candidate_sources.snippet: Maize dwarf mosaic virus (MDMV) is a serious maize pathogen, epidemic worldwide, and one of the most common virus diseases. Infected plants show mosaic patches of light and dark green color on leaves, and plants show chlorosis and stunting. Transmitted by aphid species in a non-persistent manner.

candidate_sources.title: Maize Dwarf Mosaic Virus
candidate_sources.snippet: MDMV belongs to the genus Potyvirus (Potyviridae) and was first identified in 1964 in Illinois. Symptoms often begin as chlorotic spots and streaks on young leaves, which later develop into a mottle or mosaic pattern. The use of resistant hybrids should be the first option to prevent the disease.

candidate_sources.title: Maize Dwarf Mosaic / Corn / UC Statewide IPM Program
candidate_sources.snippet: MDMV is a single stranded positive sense RNA virus transmitted by several aphid species in a non-persistent manner. MDMV can also be seed transmitted with rates up to 0.5%. Management includes use of resistant hybrids and eradicating Johnsongrass within and adjacent to maize fields early in the season.

candidate_sources.title: Corn Lethal Necrosis
candidate_sources.snippet: Corn lethal necrosis develops when two viruses occur together in the same plant. The disease causes long yellow stripes on leaves which are wider than those of maize streak virus disease. As the disease advances, maize leaves become yellow and dry out from the outside edges towards the midrib, causing dwarfing, premature aging, and potentially 100% yield loss.

candidate_sources.title: Maize lethal necrosis | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: Maize lethal necrosis (MLN) is a viral disease affecting maize (corn) caused by coinfection of maize with maize chlorotic mottle virus (MCMV) and one of several viruses from the Potyviridae family, such as sugarcane mosaic virus, maize dwarf mosaic virus, Johnsongrass mosaic virus or wheat streak mosaic virus. The CABI datasheet covers Identity, Overview, Distribution, Dispersal, Hosts/Species Affected, Diagnosis, Biology & Ecology, Seedborne Aspects, Impacts, Prevention/Control, and Further Information.

candidate_sources.title: Maize Lethal Necrosis (MLN), an Emerging Threat to Maize-Based Food Security in Sub-Saharan Africa
candidate_sources.snippet: Maize Lethal Necrosis (MLN) is an emerging, synergistic viral disease caused by coinfection of maize with maize chlorotic mottle virus (MCMV) and one of several viruses from the Potyviridae family. MLN results in leaf necrosis, premature aging, and even whole plant death, causing up to 100% losses in yield. The disease is transmitted through soil, seed, and via arthropod vectors.

candidate_sources.title: Maize streak virus (streak disease of maize) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: MSV is a serious constraint to maize production throughout sub-Saharan Africa, Egypt and islands in the Indian Ocean. Symptoms appear on the leaves 3-7 days after inoculation as pale spots or flecks, 0.5-2 mm in diameter. Symptomatology may vary depending on the host, cultivar or virus isolate. In severe cases, the initial pale spots become longer streaks which eventually coalesce.

candidate_sources.title: Maize streak virus: an old and complex 'emerging' pathogen
candidate_sources.snippet: In infected maize plants, streak disease initially manifests as minute, pale, circular spots on the lowest exposed portion of the youngest leaves. As the disease progresses, newer leaves emerge containing streaks up to several millimetres in length along the leaf veins. Lesion colour generally varies from white to yellow, with some virus strains causing red pigmentation. It is obligately transmitted by leafhopper species in the Genus Cicadulina. The development and use of streak-resistant cultivars is probably the most effective means of preventing streak epidemics.

candidate_sources.title: Management of maize streak virus
candidate_sources.snippet: Management strategies include: Uprooting infected plants when they first show signs of disease will keep the disease from spreading to healthy plants. Keep fields free from weeds, in particular grasses, to reduce disease transmission. Remove cereal crop residues since they serve as an infection source. Use resistant cultivars as the most effective and economically viable means of preventing streak epidemics.

candidate_sources.title: Details of DPV Maize white line mosaic virus and References
candidate_sources.snippet: Infected plants are severely stunted, with leaves showing a bright mosaic consisting of white, yellow and yellow-green rectangular to linear (1-2 cm) patches and stripes. The symptoms are not confined to whorl leaves (as are those of maize dwarf mosaic virus), but are present in all leaves and persist after pollination. The virus is transmitted in a soilborne manner. The vector is unknown but could be a fungus because transmission was not abolished by air drying infective soil and was prevented or decreased by treating the soil with benomyl.

candidate_sources.title: Plant Disease 1982 - Maize White Line Mosaic Virus in Ohio
candidate_sources.snippet: Maize White Line Mosaic Virus detected in Ohio. Yield losses range from 5 to 45% in infected fields. The disease is associated with wet, poorly drained soils and has been reported from East and North Central USA.

candidate_sources.title: Maize white line mosaic virus - Wikipedia
candidate_sources.snippet: Maize white line mosaic virus (MWLMV) is a member of the Aureusvirus genus. The virus has 35 nm isometric particles sedimenting as a single component, and containing a single ssRNA species. Some MWLMV isolates are associated with a satellite virus (SMWLMV).
diseases_mentioned: Maize White Line Mosaic Satellite Virus

candidate_sources.title: Nigrospora Ear Rot Cob Rot
candidate_sources.snippet: Dark gray or black mold on and between kernels; small black fungal spores on kernel surface at tip end of ear; kernels slightly bleached with white streaks; infected ears weigh less and are chaffy with loose kernels on cob; cobs with brown, tattered appearance at shank. Caused by Nigrospora oryzae, a weak pathogen that attacks plants stressed by drought, frost, root injury, diseases, or insects. Fungus survives on corn residue year-to-year.

candidate_sources.title: Nigrospora Ear and Cob Rot - Bayer Crop Science
candidate_sources.snippet: Fungal disease caused by Nigrospora oryzae with dark gray or black fungal mycelia on and between kernels, small black spores forming at kernel tips, and bleached kernels with white streaks from tips to crowns. Disease development favored by plant stress; weak pathogen attacks plants damaged prematurely by drought, frost, root injury, diseases, and insects. Management includes reducing plant stress through optimal fertility, effective insect management, avoiding corn-on-corn rotations, and proper drying and storage practices.

candidate_sources.title: Nigrospora Ear Rot | Troubleshooting Abnormal Corn Ears
candidate_sources.snippet: Nigrospora ear rot is characterized by gray fungal growth on corn kernels and small black spores. As a weak pathogen, N. oryzae attacks corn plants stressed or weakened by other diseases or environmental factors. Although this disease does not produce mycotoxins harmful to humans and livestock, it can cause considerable damage to ears, kernels, and cobs, reducing yield and quality.

candidate_sources.title: Pantoea stewartii (bacterial wilt of maize) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: Pantoea stewartii causes bacterial wilt of maize. The disease occurs in two phases: (i) wilt of seedlings when plants are systemically infected and usually die when infected at the seedling stage, and (ii) leaf blight phase where bacteria enter the xylem and cause long linear yellow-grey lesions with wavy margins that run parallel to leaf veins. Includes host range, distribution, dispersal, diagnosis, biology & ecology, and management strategies.

candidate_sources.title: Pantoea stewartii - Bugwoodwiki
candidate_sources.snippet: Pantoea stewartii subsp. stewartii is a Gram-negative, motile, yellow pigmented bacterium that causes Stewart's wilt and leaf scorch of corn. The corn flea beetle (Chaetocnema pulicaria) is the primary vector. Early-maturing sweet corn varieties and elite inbred maize lines are particularly susceptible. Disease transmission occurs via scratching wounds created by beetle feeding.

candidate_sources.title: Pantoea stewartii subsp. stewartii: lessons learned from a xylem-dwelling pathogen of sweet corn
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive peer-reviewed review of Pantoea stewartii subsp. stewartii covering pathogen characterization, symptom development in seedling wilt phase and leaf blight phase, xylem colonization mechanisms, vector biology (corn flea beetle), and disease management strategies. Discusses the unusual biology of this xylem-dwelling pathogen.

candidate_sources.title: Penicillium Ear Rot of Corn
candidate_sources.snippet: Penicillium ear rot is characterized by blue-green powdery mold growing between corn kernels, usually at the tip of the ear. Caused by Penicillium spp. Can be distinguished from other ear rots by its distinctive blue hue, and is the only ear rot resulting in blue eye of corn. Found on ears injured mechanically, by insects or hail. Managed by reducing insect wounding and maintaining low moisture in stored grain.

candidate_sources.title: HPIPM: Penicillium Seedling Blight SC
candidate_sources.snippet: Penicillium seedling blight of corn is caused by soilborne fungi. Seedlings become blighted one to two weeks after emergence with marginal scorching and dying. Examination of the hypocotyl area immediately above the seed shows a green fungal growth associated with rotted areas. Penicillium tends to infect plants prior to nodal root development and is generally favored by higher temperatures.

candidate_sources.title: Potential disease problems in corn following corn | Iowa State University Integrated Crop Management
candidate_sources.snippet: Penicillium is one of several fungi causing seedling problems in corn. The roots and mesocotyl of Penicillium-infected plants may be discolored and rotted. Symptoms include browning of leaf tips and yellowing. Penicillium tends to infect plants prior to nodal root development. Seed treatments will be necessary to ensure a healthy stand in conditions favorable for seedling diseases.

candidate_sources.title: Corn (Zea mays)-Seed Rot, Damping-off, and Seedling Blight | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Penicillium spp. commonly cause seedling diseases in corn. The fungus causes rot of seeds and seedlings, with aboveground symptoms including stunting, yellowing, wilting, and death. Blue-green fungal growth may be visible on infected seeds. Penicillium is favored by high temperatures and tends to infect plants before nodal root development.

candidate_sources.title: Physoderma Brown Spot and Stalk Rot
candidate_sources.snippet: Physoderma brown spot (PBS) and physoderma stalk rot (PSR) are fungal diseases caused by the Physoderma maydis pathogen, the only class of fungi that produce zoospores with flagella. Plants are most susceptible during early vegetative growth (V5 to V9 stages). Infection commonly occurs in the plant whorl where water accumulates. Symptoms appear prior to tasseling. Temperature requirements are 73 to 86°F with combination of sunlight, water, and moisture.

candidate_sources.title: Physoderma Stalk Rot of Corn
candidate_sources.snippet: Physoderma stalk rot is caused by the fungus Physoderma maydis. Symptoms include blackening of lower stalk nodes and potential stalk rot of the pith, which can result in breakage at the node. The pathogen survives in overwintering structures called sporangia that can remain viable for 2-7 years in crop residue. Management strategies include crop rotation, tillage, and resistant varieties.

candidate_sources.title: Dark Lesions on Corn are Purple Leaf Sheath
candidate_sources.snippet: Purple leaf sheath is common in corn fields; however, does not threaten yield potential. Purple leaf sheath symptoms include purplish-black lesions primarily on the leaf sheath and is not treatable with a fungicide. The lesion color varies from purple to brown to black. Yeast, Alternaria (a fungus), and other organisms have been recovered from the symptoms, but they are not consistently associated with the condition and rather are saprophytes or secondary invaders.

candidate_sources.title: Purple Leaf Sheath in Corn
candidate_sources.snippet: Purple leaf sheath is a harmless disorder that results when pollen or other debris become trapped in the leaf sheaths by the stalk. A variety of saprophytic fungi, bacteria, and yeast feed on the trapped pollen and the result is a purple to brown spot on the leaf sheath or stalk where the decomposition of the pollen is occurring. No discoloration is associated with the internal stalk tissue and no management is required.

candidate_sources.title: Sweet Corn Diseases and Control Measures
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive guide covering sweet corn diseases including Purple Leaf Sheath, with information on symptoms, pathogen identification, and management recommendations for various corn diseases.

candidate_sources.title: Pythium Root Rot
candidate_sources.snippet: Mild to moderately infected seedlings often are stunted and grow more slowly than healthy seedlings. The mesocotyls of infected seedlings are often rotted instead of being healthy, firm, and white in color. Infected plants typically have brown, rotted roots and mesocotyl.

candidate_sources.title: Nine Species of Pythium Associated with Corn Seeding Blight in Southeastern Iowa
candidate_sources.snippet: Iowa State researchers recovered nine species of Pythium from affected fields with P. torulosum being the most prevalent species. Cool soil temperatures (55°F) favor both seed and root rot caused by P. torulosum. Metalaxyl and mefenoxam seed treatments have excellent activity against Pythium species.

candidate_sources.title: Disease Caused by Pythium (Pythium)
candidate_sources.snippet: Educational module on Pythium disease with information on pathogen identification, symptoms including dark slimy lesions on roots and mesocotyls, and management including seed treatments and cultural practices.

candidate_sources.title: Pythium and Other Seedling Diseases in Crops
candidate_sources.snippet: University of Nebraska CropWatch extension article covering Pythium seedling diseases in crops including symptom identification, favorable conditions (cold wet soils), and management through seed treatments with metalaxyl, mefenoxam, or ethaboxam.

candidate_sources.title: Conditions Favor Seedling Diseases in Early Planted Corn and Soybeans
candidate_sources.snippet: Nebraska extension article on early-planted corn seedling diseases including Pythium, covering environmental conditions that favor infection and management strategies for cold, wet soils.

candidate_sources.title: Pythium root and stem rot - Plant & Pest Diagnostics
candidate_sources.snippet: Pythium root and stem rot is a common disease of corn seedlings that causes stunted, slower growing plants, to severely infected dead plants with brown, rotted roots and mesocotyl. Stand reduction is typically seen in low-lying, wet regions of the field. Disease is caused by many species of oomycete pathogen Pythium, with over 15 species identified in the Mid-Atlantic region.

candidate_sources.title: Pythium Root Rot in Corn – Maryland Agronomy News
candidate_sources.snippet: University of Maryland extension resource on Pythium root rot in corn. Discusses yield impacts with research showing infected plants yielding approximately 84 bu/acre while healthy plants averaged 219 bu/acre. Covers pathogen biology, disease identification, and integrated pest management strategies.

candidate_sources.title: Pythium Stalk Rot - UC Statewide IPM Program
candidate_sources.snippet: Pythium stalk rot causes distorted stalk tissue with one or more of the lowest internodes turning tan to brown and becoming water soaked, soft, or slimy. Caused by Pythium species, an oomycete pathogen favored by extended soil wetness. Disease typically evident shortly before or after tasseling, most common in low spots with poor drainage.

candidate_sources.title: Corn Disease Profile II: Stalk Rot Diseases - UNL Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Extension plant pathology team resource documenting stalk rot diseases of corn with detailed information on Pythium and other stalk rot pathogens, including identification of symptoms, disease cycle, and management strategies.

candidate_sources.title: Corn Seedling Disease Identification and Management
candidate_sources.snippet: Rhizoctonia species cause seedling diseases with brown lesions on the mesocotyl and roots of seedlings that can girdle and rot off roots. Initial symptoms are brown lesions that can cause damping-off. The most distinctive symptoms are reddish brown sunken cankers on roots, crown, and brace roots of larger plants. Rhizoctonia can infect corn roots between 46 to 82 °F.

candidate_sources.title: Corn Seedling Diseases 2015
candidate_sources.snippet: Rhizoctonia is one of the most common fungal pathogens causing seedling rots in corn. Brown lesions appear on the mesocotyl and roots, with plants becoming stunted or chlorotic. Rhizoctonia species tend to be more common in drier growing conditions and more severe in irrigated corn. The pathogen can cause crown rot and brace root rot on older plants.

candidate_sources.title: Rhizoctonia root and stem rot on soybean
candidate_sources.snippet: Rhizoctonia solani causes root and stem rot diseases. The fungal pathogen infects many different plants in the northern U.S., affecting roots and causing brown lesions on the mesocotyl. Initial symptoms include damping-off in seedlings. Rhizoctonia-infected plants may be stunted or chlorotic, but often there are no aboveground symptoms. Seed treatment fungicides provide protection against Rhizoctonia solani.
diseases_mentioned: Rhizoctonia solani root and stem rot

candidate_sources.title: Rhizoctonia solani - Plant & Pest Diagnostics
candidate_sources.snippet: Rhizoctonia solani is a fungal pathogen causing root and crown rot diseases. The pathogen affects corn, soybeans, and other vegetable crops. Rhizoctonia solani AGs can cause crown rot and brace root rot on corn leading to lodging. Environmental conditions favoring infection include soil temperatures between 46-82°F and adequate soil moisture.

candidate_sources.title: Rhizopus rot - Integrated Pest Management
candidate_sources.snippet: Rhizopus rot is a common postharvest disease characterized by rapid, watery decay covered by coarse gray mycelium with black sporangia. Symptoms include water-soaked spots that enlarge rapidly, and prevention focuses on temperature control (below 46-50°F stops growth), minimizing wounds, and field sanitation.

candidate_sources.title: Rhizopus Soft Rot of Sweetpotato | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Rhizopus soft rot, caused by the necrotrophic fungus Rhizopus stolonifer, affects numerous crops including corn. Symptoms are watery areas quickly covered by coarse gray hairy mycelia with black sporangia. The fungus lacks cutinases and enters tissue only through wounds. Management includes rapid cooling, wound prevention, field sanitation, and fungicide use.

candidate_sources.title: Rhizopus stolonifer
candidate_sources.snippet: Rhizopus stolonifer is a ubiquitous necrotrophic Zygomycete fungus causing postharvest soft rot on more than 200 fruit and vegetable crops including cereals like corn. Disease features gray fungal mycelium with black sporangia resembling 'grey man's beard'. Environmental factors favor disease progression at elevated temperatures (25-29°C).

candidate_sources.title: Fusarium Root Rot in Corn | CropWatch | Nebraska
candidate_sources.snippet: Fusarium root rot symptoms generally include dark brown to black, discolored, decaying or completely rotted roots. Several Fusarium spp are known to cause root rots in corn. Management recommendations include selecting hybrids with good Fusarium root rot ratings, controlling root worms and other insects causing injury to roots, improving soil drainage, and using fungicide seed treatment.

candidate_sources.title: Root Rots of Corn
candidate_sources.snippet: Corn root rots are very common and are caused by several soilborne pathogens such as Pythium, Fusarium, and Rhizoctonia spp. Aboveground symptoms include stunting, uneven growth, chlorosis, small or poorly filled ears, or wilting. Initially, small yellow-brown lesions develop on roots; roots later turn dark brown and are obviously decayed. Fine roots slough off after rotting. Root rot is generally reduced by standard seed fungicide treatments on corn.

candidate_sources.title: Corn Smut | USU Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Spores are spread through wind or water splashing to nearby plants. The pathogen overwinters in crop debris or soil and can remain viable for several years. Management includes resistant varieties, cultural practices to avoid plant wounding, and removal of galls before they break open.

candidate_sources.title: Southern Corn Leaf Blight of Corn
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive encyclopedia entry covering Southern Corn Leaf Blight (SCLB) caused by Bipolaris maydis, including symptoms on leaves and ears, environmental conditions (warm temps 68-90°F and high humidity), and management strategies including host resistance breeding and crop debris management

candidate_sources.title: Helminthosporium Leaf Blights of Sweet Corn
candidate_sources.snippet: Illinois Extension factsheet on Helminthosporium leaf blights (older taxonomic name for Bipolaris maydis), detailing symptoms including oblong tan to grayish lesions with purplish-brown borders, ear infections with gray-black lesions, and management through crop rotation and resistant varieties

candidate_sources.title: Southern Corn Leaf Blight: A Story Worth Retelling
candidate_sources.snippet: USDA ARS research publication on the history and biology of Southern Corn Leaf Blight caused by Bipolaris maydis (Cochliobolus heterostrophus), covering disease symptoms ranging from minute specks to 1.5-inch lesions, seedling blight, and management through resistance breeding and residue management

candidate_sources.title: RPD No. 202 - Plant Disease - University of Illinois
candidate_sources.snippet: University of Illinois extension factsheet on Southern Corn Leaf Blight caused by Bipolaris maydis. Details symptoms including tan-gray centered lesions, management through resistant varieties, fungicide application at tasseling to silking stages, and cultural practices including crop rotation.

candidate_sources.title: Southern Corn Leaf Blight and Stalk Rot - CornipmPIPE
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive guide to Southern Corn Leaf Blight and Stalk Rot (Bipolaris maydis). Covers three races (O, C, T) with varying host ranges, favorable conditions (68-90°F, high humidity), symptom identification, fungicide options, and resistant variety selection for management.

candidate_sources.title: Southern Rust | CropWatch | Nebraska
candidate_sources.snippet: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch dedicated page providing comprehensive information on Southern Corn Rust diagnosis, environmental conditions favoring infection, and management recommendations for corn growers.

candidate_sources.title: Southern vs. Common Rust in Corn - FACT SHEET #2019002
candidate_sources.snippet: University of Florida IFAS fact sheet providing comparative analysis of Southern Rust and Common Rust symptoms, pathogen characteristics (Puccinia polysora), and management strategies specific to each disease.

candidate_sources.title: Puccinia polysora (American corn rust) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: Southern rust is caused by the obligate biotrophic fungus Puccinia polysora, and is often ranked in the top five most destructive corn diseases in the southern United States. According to an SCR distribution map published by CABI, the disease has been found in more than 110 countries spanning Africa, Asia, the Americas and Australasia.

candidate_sources.title: Common and Southern Rusts Distinguishing Between | Purdue Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Timely application of fungicides with multiple modes of action between the VT and R3 stages has been shown to reduce disease severity and protect yield. If southern rust is not observed until R3, the application can be delayed until then. Under hot humid conditions, spores of Puccinia polysora can infect susceptible corn, with symptoms observable within 3-4 days.

candidate_sources.title: Pantoea stewartii (bacterial wilt of maize) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: Pantoea stewartii subsp. stewartii causes Stewart's wilt of corn. Early-maturing sweet corn varieties and some elite inbred maize lines are particularly susceptible. The bacterium colonizes both the intercellular spaces of leaf tissue (causing characteristic water-soaked lesions) and the xylem (leading to systemic spread and wilting). Vectored by the corn flea beetle (Chaetocnema pulicaria).

candidate_sources.title: Corn Stewart's Disease | Iowa State Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Iowa State Extension publication on Corn Stewart's Disease includes information on disease symptoms, disease spread and development, temperature and flea beetle survival, and disease control strategies. Stewart's disease is caused by the bacterium Pantoea stewartii and is transmitted by corn flea beetles.

candidate_sources.title: Stewart's Wilt (Bacterial Wilt) in Corn | University of Kentucky IPM
candidate_sources.snippet: Sweet corn is much more susceptible to Stewart's wilt than field corn. Disease is characterized by pale green to yellow streaks with irregular or wavy margins that parallel leaf veins. Two phases: seedling wilt phase and leaf blight phase. Transmitted by corn flea beetles. Winter temperature forecasting: if sum of average monthly temperatures for December, January, and February is less than 90°F, disease pressure will be mild.

candidate_sources.title: Corn Diseases: Symptoms, Scouting, and Management | Iowa State Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive Iowa State Extension resource covering corn diseases including Stewart's disease symptoms and management. Lists long, pale-green to yellow-gray streaks with wavy margins on leaves. Management includes using resistant hybrids, monitoring winter temperatures for disease pressure prediction, and controlling corn flea beetle vectors.

candidate_sources.title: Stewart's Wilt in Sweet Corn - Michigan State University Extension Factsheet
candidate_sources.snippet: Extension factsheet detailing Stewart's wilt symptoms including seedling wilt phase and leaf blight phase, with characteristic pale green to yellow streaks and irregular margins following leaf veins. Covers life cycle of the corn flea beetle vector (Chaetocnema pulicaria), disease management through resistant varieties, and cultural practices.

candidate_sources.title: Stewart's wilt of corn - APS Network Education Center
candidate_sources.snippet: APS publication providing detailed information on Stewart's wilt caused by Pantoea stewartii, including two-phase symptom presentation (wilt phase in seedlings, leaf blight phase in mature plants), pathogen biology, vector transmission by corn flea beetles, and integrated management approaches including resistant hybrids and seed certification.

candidate_sources.title: Sugarcane Mosaic Disease: Characteristics, Identification and Management
candidate_sources.snippet: A comprehensive peer-reviewed study on Sugarcane Mosaic Virus covering characteristics, identification methods, and management strategies. SCMV is a plant pathogenic virus of the family Potyviridae affecting corn, sorghum, and other grass species.

candidate_sources.title: Lethal Viral Necrosis (associated with Sugarcane Mosaic Virus-SCMV) Frequently Asked Questions
candidate_sources.snippet: UF/IFAS Extension resource providing frequently asked questions about Lethal Viral Necrosis associated with Sugarcane Mosaic Virus. Covers symptoms, epidemiology, and management approaches for corn growers.

candidate_sources.title: Tar Spot of Corn | VCE Publications | Virginia Tech
candidate_sources.snippet: Extension factsheet detailing symptoms (yellow to tan flecks with black glossy stromata), pathogen Phyllachora maydis, and management strategies including fungicide applications and crop rotation

candidate_sources.title: Be On Lookout for Tar Spot: A New Disease of Corn | University of Maryland Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: University of Maryland Extension resource on tar spot identification, spread conditions (air temperatures 16-23°C, humidity >75%), and management recommendations for North American corn production

candidate_sources.title: Tar Spot of Corn: A Diagnostic and Methods Guide | Plant Health Progress
candidate_sources.snippet: Peer-reviewed APS publication providing comprehensive diagnostic procedures, symptom descriptions, pathogen biology, and evidence-based management methods for tar spot disease

candidate_sources.title: An Overview of Tar Spot
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive overview documenting yield losses (25-30% in Midwest, up to 60 bu/acre in severe cases), pathogen overwinter survival in crop residue, and integrated management including tolerance breeding and fungicides

candidate_sources.title: Trichoderma Ear Rot of Corn
candidate_sources.snippet: Trichoderma ear rot is caused by Trichoderma viride and appears as dark green mold growing on or between kernels, often covering the entire ear. The abundant thick greenish mold growing on and between the kernels makes Trichoderma ear rot very easy to distinguish from Diplodia, Fusarium, and Gibberella ear rots. Kernels may sprout on the cob if disease is severe. It is primarily found on scattered plants under severe stress and is associated with injury to developing ears.

candidate_sources.title: Trichoderma viride | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI Compendium datasheet covering Identity, Hosts/Species Affected, Distribution, Symptoms, Pathogen, Conditions for Development, and Further Information on Trichoderma viride, the causal agent of Trichoderma ear rot in corn and other crops.

candidate_sources.title: Is Trichoderma ear rot on maize really a new dangerous plant disease? - Frontiers in Agronomy
candidate_sources.snippet: Peer-reviewed article examining Trichoderma as an emerging disease on maize. Describes Trichoderma ear rot characterized by dark green to grey-green mold between kernels and on husks. Discusses whether Trichoderma is a primary pathogen or secondary invader.

candidate_sources.title: Trichoderma Ear Rot - Ohio State University
candidate_sources.snippet: Ohio State University troubleshooting guide for abnormal corn ears, including Trichoderma ear rot identification and management. Describes symptoms and disease characteristics.

candidate_sources.title: Effect of Trichoderma harzianum on maize rhizosphere microbiome and biocontrol of Fusarium Stalk rot - Nature Scientific Reports
candidate_sources.snippet: Peer-reviewed research examining Trichoderma harzianum as a biocontrol agent against Fusarium stalk rot of maize. Reports antagonistic activity of 96.30% and disease reduction of 86.66% in biocontrol trials.

candidate_sources.title: Infection cycle of maize stalk rot and ear rot caused by Fusarium verticillioides
candidate_sources.snippet: Fusarium verticillioides causes stalk rot, ear rot, and seedling blight in maize. The infection cycle shows hyphae infecting plants from radical to stem and extending to ear, with fumonisin B₁ production necessary for seedling blight manifestation. F. verticillioides acts as a hemibiotroph and endophyte.

candidate_sources.title: Fusarium Disease of Maize and Its Management through Sustainable Approach
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive coverage of Fusarium diseases in maize including seedling blight and ear rot caused by Fusarium verticillioides and related species. Discusses disease cycle, management through cultural practices (crop residue burial, crop rotation), and chemical control with azoles.

candidate_sources.title: Xanthomonas vasicola pv. vasculorum (bacterial leaf streak of corn) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive CABI datasheet covering identity, distribution, dispersal, hosts affected, diagnosis, biology & ecology, impacts, and prevention/control measures for Xanthomonas vasicola pv. vasculorum causing bacterial leaf streak of corn.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Leaf Streak of Corn - ISU Extension Store
candidate_sources.snippet: Iowa State University extension resource on bacterial leaf streak of corn caused by Xanthomonas vasicola pv. vasculorum, covering identification, symptoms, pathogen characteristics, and management recommendations for field corn, seed corn, popcorn and sweet corn.
